On my way home, my senior associate texted me again, asking for our client's billing information, something she could have done herself since she has their contacts. I forwarded the information as she asked. When I got home, I took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked to wake up to 2 missed calls and 30 new messages from her, giving me work to do from home. I felt it was unfair for her to assign me work while I was on sick leave, so I ignored the messages and didn't reply. Now, the question is: Am I in the wrong (AITA) for not replying to her texts? Let me break this down. First, I was sick and had notified her, so I was entitled to take a sick leave. She allowed me the leave, which is good. However, she continued to text me with work-related tasks, which I tried to ignore to rest. She called me, and I responded to that urgent request, but then she kept texting me even after I informed her I was going to the doctor and wouldn't have my laptop. Ignoring her texts after that point seems justified because I was trying to rest and recover, especially since the doctor had advised me to take it easy due to overwork. It's important to prioritize my health, especially when I'm already overworked. However, in a professional setting, ignoring texts from a senior associate might be seen as unprofessional or insubordinate. But in this case, I had already communicated my situation, and she continued to assign work despite knowing I was unwell and trying to rest. I also forwarded the billing information when she asked, showing that I was still trying to be helpful despite my illness. The sheer number of messages she sent after that might indicate that she was either unaware of my condition or was expecting me to work despite being sick. Considering all this, I think it's reasonable to ignore her texts after a certain point to prioritize my health and well-being. It's important to set boundaries, especially when one's health is at risk due to overwork. But I'm also aware that in some workplaces, ignoring communications from seniors, even when unwell, might have consequences. It's a tricky situation because I need to balance my health with professional responsibilities. Maybe a better approach would have been to respond to her initial texts, explain my situation again, and politely decline to take on more work while I'm recovering. That way, I maintain professionalism while also taking care of my health. In conclusion, while ignoring her texts might seem like the right choice to rest, it's also important to communicate my situation clearly to avoid misunderstandings and potential professional repercussions.
